title: More than a place to eat: Inside Cavite’s thriving food bazaar culture
summary: In Mendez, Cavite, local bazaars do more than bring the community together over food — they also help young entrepreneurs earn extra income and gain real-world business experience

blocks.text: For some residents, a visit to the food bazaar means satisfying a craving for takoyaki, fries, or milk tea.For local entrepreneurs, the stalls offer something more: an opportunity to introduce their products, find new customers, and turn a small business into a growing livelihood.

What began as an initiative to give local merchants a place to sell their products has grown into a gathering of food entrepreneurs and customers in Mendez, Cavite.For Alvin Dimaranan, one of the organizers of the food bazaars, the initiative started with a small group of entrepreneurs looking for opportunities to promote their businesses.
“We were just a few, but we pushed through,” he recalled, describing how they initially gathered around 18 merchants for the Mendez Day celebration in 2018.

Dimaranan, who is also known as Vindims, documented the preparations and opening of the bazaar through his vlogs.The videos eventually gained traction on Facebook, reaching almost two million views over several weeks. The unexpected turnout encouraged more entrepreneurs to participate.From its initial group of merchants, the organization has since grown to approximately 123 to 125 businesses, according to Dimaranan.
“If I want to grow a business, it could just be me,” he said. “But my concept is a food bazaar, so there should be more merchants who can benefit.”
For some business owners, participating in the bazaars means reaching customers who might otherwise never discover their products.

Jhon Christian Atienza, owner of Jacob’s Milk Tea, established his business on March 8, 2023. He joined the Mendez food bazaars to introduce his products to a wider audience, gain customer feedback, and make his business more recognizable.
Through the events, Atienza said, customers who initially purchased out of curiosity eventually became regular patrons.

For him, the benefits extend beyond the sales made during the bazaar.Some customers have also recommended his business to their families and friends, helping him reach more potential buyers through word of mouth.
He considers these recommendations valuable because they help establish relationships that continue even after the bazaar ends.
A similar experience comes from Jefferson Hondo, owner of Chambee Mendez, which opened in March 2026.

Hondo joined the bazaar to promote his store not only to Mendez residents but also to visitors from neighboring towns.He said the exposure helped the business attract regular customers who first encountered the brand during the event.
Because people intentionally visit bazaars to explore different food offerings, Hondo said promoting the business and generating sales became easier.
For Mark Anthony Arania, owner of Leonora’s, the bazaar similarly provides an opportunity to introduce his business’ pasta dishes to more residents.
Established on July 7, 2021, Leonora joined to expand its reach within Mendez.Arania said participation helped the business gain recognition and attract more customers.
While some entrepreneurs participate to expand existing businesses, others see the bazaars as a means of supporting their daily needs.
Arlyssa Siagan, owner of Kopi’s Long Fries, started her business on December 1, 2024.As a college student, she joined the bazaar primarily to help cover her educational expenses.
The income she earned also contributed, even partially, to her family’s needs.
Beyond the financial assistance, Siagan said the experience taught her how to interact with customers and manage a business.
However, balancing entrepreneurship and academics also required sacrifices, particularly in managing her time.
She said the opportunity to participate in bazaars demonstrates how small business ventures can provide students with an additional source of income while allowing them to develop practical skills.
Meanwhile, Dela Pendon, owner of Edna’s Puto Bumbong, has been operating her business for 10 years. She joins bazaars to promote her products and encourage more customers to patronize them.
For customers Nic and Frankie, visiting the food bazaar has become part of their routine, with the two going approximately twice a week.
Aside from the food choices, they said the bazaar offers a nearby place to eat, hang out, and spend time with friends.
They also identified Jacob’s Milk Tea as one of the businesses they continued supporting after discovering it through the bazaar.
They believe these events help residents become more familiar with local businesses, encouraging them to visit restaurants and stores even when the bazaars are no longer operating.
More than providing access to different food offerings, they said, the gatherings create opportunities for residents to interact, reconnect with friends, and spend time with their families.

For Dimaranan, the benefits also extend beyond the merchants.Organizing a bazaar creates opportunities for street sweepers, garbage collectors, barangay tanods, and local performers, including singers, bands, and dance groups.
The organizers also incorporate performances into their events, with contributions from participating merchants helping provide compensation for local talents.
The local government also recognizes the bazaars as part of its efforts to support micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs).

Ronald Perey, chief of staff of the Mendez local government, said the initiative provides local food producers and entrepreneurs with an opportunity to introduce their products to the public within a shorter period.
Perey identified December 2022 as the beginning of the municipality’s involvement in recognizing and supporting the initiative under Mayor Cocoy Mendoza’s administration.
He said the LGU hopes that greater product recognition can eventually encourage businesses to increase production, expand their operations, and generate employment opportunities.

The municipality also plans to provide starting capital assistance to encourage more entrepreneurs to establish or sustain their businesses.Perey cited the Sustainable Livelihood Program and the municipality’s investment policies as other forms of support.
However, opportunities to participate in the bazaars are not without limitations.

Hondo pointed out that organizers restrict the number of participating businesses because of limited space and the need to manage competition among vendors offering similar products. This means not every entrepreneur who wants to join can secure a stall.
Dimaranan also identified unpredictable weather, daily rental fees, and utility expenses as challenges, particularly when rain discourages customers from visiting.
Despite these difficulties, the bazaars continue to provide a shared platform for entrepreneurs to reach customers and introduce their products.

In Mendez, a food bazaar may last only a few days. But for the entrepreneurs who bring their products to the stalls, the relationships and opportunities they build can continue long after the tents come down. – Rappler.com
Neo Croox is a Rappler intern from the University of Santo Tomas.
